blocks.content: TCP and UDP are both layer 4 transport protocols, both carry data between two applications using port numbers, and both sit directly on top of IP. Beyond that, they make completely opposite trade-offs, TCP prioritizes correctness, UDP prioritizes speed.

TCP guarantees your data arrives complete, in order, and without corruption. UDP just sends packets and hopes for the best. Choosing between them comes down to whether your application can tolerate losing a little data in exchange for never waiting on it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273378899-568273850.png
blocks.alt: The same job, moving data between two applications, solved with two deliberately opposite priorities

blocks.content: 1. TCP: Connection-Oriented and Reliable

TCP is connection oriented. Before a single byte of application data moves, both sides complete a handshake to establish shared state, the same three-way handshake covered in depth in the OSI Model topic, SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, after which TCP tracks every segment sent, confirms every one received, and retransmits anything that goes missing.
What TCP Gives You on Top of Raw IP
blocks.text: What TCP Gives You on Top of Raw IP

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273381014-230987718.png
blocks.alt: TCP turns unreliable, unordered IP packets into one clean, ordered stream the application can trust completely

blocks.content: Raw IP packets can arrive out of order, get duplicated, or simply vanish, IP itself makes no promises at all. TCP fixes every one of these problems. With reliable delivery, the sender breaks data into numbered segments, and if the receiver notices a gap, it asks for exactly that missing segment again. With ordering, segments are reassembled in their original sequence before the application ever sees them, regardless of what order they actually arrived in.
Tearing a Connection Down
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273382733-536349432.png
blocks.alt: Closing a TCP connection takes four steps, since each side's own data stream has to be closed independently

blocks.content: Closing a TCP connection takes four steps rather than three, because each side has its own independent stream that must be closed separately. The client sends a FIN, signaling it is done sending. The server acknowledges, finishes whatever work remains, then sends its own FIN. The client acknowledges that too, and the connection is closed, with the client waiting briefly in a final state to absorb any last, delayed, duplicate packets before fully forgetting the connection.
2. UDP: Connectionless and Fast
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273384449-792487439.png
blocks.alt: UDP simply stuffs data into a datagram and sends it, with no handshake and no guarantee of anything

blocks.content: UDP is connectionless. No handshake, no acknowledgments, no retransmissions, no ordering. Data goes into a datagram, gets aimed at a destination, and gets sent, whether it actually arrives is not UDP's concern at all.

That sounds like a weakness, but for many applications it is exactly what is wanted. No handshake means no round trip delay before the first byte moves. No retransmission means never waiting on data that is already stale by the time it would arrive.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024509-922440648.png
blocks.alt: UDP delivers whatever survives the trip and moves on, a lost datagram is never retried automatically

blocks.content: Sending datagrams 1, 2, and 3, datagram 1 might reach the server, datagram 2 might get lost in the network entirely, and datagram 3 might still arrive successfully. UDP does not notice or care, there are no acknowledgments and no retransmissions, the receiving application simply gets whatever showed up, in this case 1 and 3, with no ordering guarantee either.

blocks.title: Reliability Becomes the Application's Job
blocks.content: Because UDP guarantees nothing, the application itself decides what to do about missing data, ignore the loss entirely, request a resend manually, or simply continue, exactly the choice video streaming and gaming both make deliberately.

3. When Each One Is the Right Choice
blocks.text: 3. When Each One Is the Right Choice

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024988-694103246.png
blocks.alt: UDP fits whenever a little loss is cheaper than the delay reliability would cost

blocks.content: A DNS query is a single packet asking a question and a single packet answering it. Using TCP would mean a full handshake, the query, the response, and a teardown, five or more packets for what is fundamentally a two packet job. UDP does it in two packets with zero setup cost, and if the reply is lost, the resolver simply asks again.

DNS is a genuinely instructive edge case here too, it actually falls back to TCP specifically when a response is too large to fit in a single UDP datagram, showing the two protocols are not always an exclusive either or choice, even within one single system.

In a live video call, a lost audio packet is far less damaging than a delayed one. If TCP retransmitted a dropped voice packet, it would arrive perhaps two hundred milliseconds late, and now the audio is audibly out of sync. With UDP, the lost frame is simply skipped, the conversation continues with a tiny glitch instead of a noticeable delay.

In online gaming, a player's position update from two hundred milliseconds ago is already useless, the player has moved on. Games send position updates many times a second over UDP, if one packet is lost, the very next one arrives with newer, more relevant data anyway, so retransmitting the stale one would only make the game feel sluggish.

Notice the shared pattern across every one of these cases, DNS, video, gaming, and IoT: each one has a natural, frequent supply of fresh data arriving anyway, which is exactly what makes losing one specific piece of it tolerable.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024986-266949515.png
blocks.alt: TCP fits whenever every byte genuinely matters and none of it can simply be skipped

blocks.content: When a bank transfer moves real money, every byte of that transaction must arrive correctly and in order, a dropped packet mid transfer cannot simply be skipped. Correctness matters more than the few extra milliseconds TCP's handshake and acknowledgments cost. The same reasoning applies to SSH commands, database queries, and file downloads, anywhere a missing or corrupted piece invalidates the entire operation.

blocks.title: A Fifth Case: Battery Constrained IoT Sensors
blocks.content: A battery powered sensor reporting a temperature reading every few seconds has the same incentive as a video call, avoiding TCP's handshake and acknowledgment overhead directly saves battery life, and an occasional missed reading is rarely worth the radio power a retransmission would cost.
4. QUIC: What Comes After TCP
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273391362-591130142.png
blocks.alt: One lost packet blocks every unrelated stream behind it in TCP, but only its own stream in QUIC

blocks.content: QUIC, used in HTTP/3, is built on top of UDP but implements its own reliability, ordering, and congestion control above it. Its key advantage is eliminating TCP's head of line blocking. In TCP, everything runs over one single ordered stream, so a single lost packet blocks every piece of data behind it, even entirely unrelated data like an image or a stylesheet that already arrived correctly, simply because TCP's ordering guarantee applies to the whole connection at once.

QUIC solves this by splitting data into genuinely independent streams within the same connection. If a packet is lost in one stream, only that specific stream pauses, every other stream keeps moving without waiting at all, meaningfully improving page load times on unreliable networks.
5. Flow Control and Congestion Control
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273393145-113072543.png
blocks.alt: The receiver's own advertised window tells the sender exactly how much unacknowledged data it can safely handle at once

blocks.content: TCP's reliability guarantee alone would be dangerous without a way to prevent a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver, or overwhelming the network itself. Flow control solves the first problem, the receiver continuously advertises a window size representing how much more data it can currently buffer, and the sender never sends more unacknowledged data than that window allows. If the receiver's buffer starts filling up, it advertises a smaller window, and the sender slows down to match, entirely independent of anything happening on the network in between.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273394865-866277854.png
blocks.alt: TCP grows its send rate gradually and cuts it sharply the moment it detects real congestion

blocks.content: Congestion control solves the second problem, protecting the network itself rather than just the receiver. A new TCP connection starts sending cautiously and increases its rate gradually as acknowledgments confirm the network can handle it. The moment a packet loss or timeout signals real congestion somewhere along the path, TCP cuts its send rate sharply rather than gradually, then resumes its cautious growth from that lower point. UDP does none of this at all, a UDP sender can keep blasting datagrams at a fixed rate even while the network is visibly congested, which is exactly why protocols built on UDP, including QUIC, have to implement their own congestion control independently.
6. Checksums: Verifying Corruption, Not Delivery
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024988-157021138.png
blocks.alt: Both TCP and UDP compute a checksum on every packet, silently dropping anything that arrives corrupted

blocks.content: It is easy to assume only TCP checks data integrity, but both protocols carry a checksum field, and both silently drop a packet whose checksum no longer matches its payload, a sign the data was corrupted in transit. The real difference is what happens next. TCP treats a dropped, corrupted segment exactly like a lost one, it goes unacknowledged, and the sender eventually retransmits it. UDP simply drops it and moves on, exactly as it does with ordinary packet loss, since UDP never distinguishes corruption from loss in the first place, both just mean the datagram never arrives.

9. Multicast: A Capability Only UDP Has
blocks.text: 9. Multicast: A Capability Only UDP Has

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273398182-997264499.png
blocks.alt: One UDP sender can address an entire group of receivers at once, something a connection oriented protocol structurally cannot do

blocks.content: Because TCP is connection oriented, a dedicated connection exists between exactly two endpoints, there is no natural way for one TCP sender to efficiently reach many receivers at once, it would need a separate connection, and a separate copy of the data, per receiver. UDP has no such restriction. A single UDP multicast sender can address an entire group of subscribed receivers simultaneously, the network itself replicates the packet only where it is actually needed. This is exactly how live financial market data feeds and some video distribution systems deliver identical data to thousands of receivers without sending it separately to each one.
10. Nagle's Algorithm: When TCP's Own Optimization Hurts Latency
blocks.text: 10. Nagle's Algorithm: When TCP's Own Optimization Hurts Latency

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273399996-919962020.png
blocks.alt: TCP can briefly delay small outgoing writes to bundle them into fewer, larger segments, unless that behavior is explicitly disabled

blocks.content: TCP was originally designed assuming many applications write data in small, frequent chunks, and sending a separate, mostly empty segment for each tiny chunk wastes bandwidth on header overhead. Nagle's algorithm addresses this by briefly holding small writes and bundling them into one larger segment before actually sending.

blocks.title: Why Real Time Applications Turn It Off
blocks.content: That brief bundling delay, often just tens of milliseconds, is completely invisible for a file download but genuinely noticeable for something like a remote terminal session or a competitive game sending frequent, tiny updates over TCP. That is exactly why latency sensitive applications explicitly disable Nagle's algorithm using the TCP_NODELAY socket option, trading a small amount of bandwidth efficiency for sending every byte the instant it is ready.
11. Socket Programming: SOCK_STREAM vs SOCK_DGRAM
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024984-149610405.png
blocks.alt: The choice between TCP and UDP is made at the exact moment a socket is created, through its socket type

blocks.content: This entire choice shows up directly in application code, in the type of socket that gets created. A SOCK_STREAM socket gives a connected, ordered byte stream, TCP underneath. A SOCK_DGRAM socket gives independent, connectionless datagrams, UDP underneath. Everything covered in this topic, the handshake, the guarantees, the lack of them, follows directly from that single choice made once, right when the socket is opened.

import socket

# TCP: a connected, ordered byte stream
tcp_socket = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)

# UDP: independent, connectionless datagrams
udp_socket = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)

blocks.content: 12. The Real Cost of the Handshake
blocks.text: 12. The Real Cost of the Handshake

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273403371-598969158.png
blocks.alt: TCP spends a full round trip on its handshake before any real data moves, UDP sends the first useful byte immediately

blocks.content: TCP's three way handshake is not free, it costs one full network round trip before a single byte of actual application data can be sent. On a link with 150 milliseconds of round trip latency, that is 150 milliseconds spent purely on setup, before the real request even begins. UDP has no such cost at all, the very first datagram sent can already carry real data.

blocks.title: Where TCP Fast Open and 0-RTT Come From
blocks.content: This exact cost is why TCP Fast Open and QUIC's 0-RTT resumption exist, both let a client that has connected to a server recently skip the handshake's round trip entirely on a repeat connection, sending real data immediately while the connection is still being confirmed, at the cost of some additional complexity in guaranteeing that early data is safe to process twice.
13. MTU and Fragmentation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273405201-166491714.png
blocks.alt: TCP transparently splits large data into segments and reassembles them, UDP leaves that problem entirely to the application

blocks.content: Every network link has a maximum transmission unit, a size limit on a single packet, commonly around 1500 bytes on ordinary Ethernet. When an application hands TCP more data than fits in one segment, TCP transparently splits it into multiple segments and reassembles them correctly on the other end, the application never has to think about this at all.

UDP offers no such help. A single UDP datagram larger than the path's MTU either gets fragmented at the IP layer, a fragile process where losing just one fragment invalidates the entire datagram, or is rejected outright depending on configuration. Because of this, applications sending larger payloads over UDP, like a video streaming protocol, deliberately keep each individual datagram under the MTU themselves, splitting large frames into several small application level packets, rather than relying on IP fragmentation at all.

blocks.title: Why This Matters for Real Time Media
blocks.content: A streaming protocol that lets IP fragmentation handle an oversized UDP datagram risks losing the entire frame if even one small fragment goes missing, exactly the kind of silent, avoidable failure that careful protocol design at the application layer exists to prevent.
14. A Common Mistake: Defaulting to TCP by Habit
blocks.text: 14. A Common Mistake: Defaulting to TCP by Habit

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024988-977836298.png
blocks.alt: Building a live video feed on TCP by default works fine until the first packet loss, at which point retransmission itself becomes the problem

blocks.content: A frequent design mistake is reaching for TCP purely out of habit, because it sounds more reliable, without asking what the application actually needs. A live video feed built on TCP looks completely fine in a demo with no packet loss. The moment a real network drops even one frame, TCP dutifully retransmits it, and that retransmitted frame now arrives late, visibly out of sync with the audio it was meant to accompany. UDP, deliberately allowing that one frame to simply be skipped, would have kept the stream feeling smooth.

blocks.title: Ask What Failure Should Look Like
blocks.content: Before picking a transport protocol, ask specifically what should happen when a packet is lost. If the honest answer is skip it and move on, UDP is very likely the right choice, no matter how unconventional that feels.

The example below simulates exactly this contrast: sending five segments where two are transiently lost on the first attempt. The reliable, TCP style sender automatically retransmits until every segment is confirmed delivered. The unreliable, UDP style sender tries once and reports only whatever actually survived.

codes.python:
def unreliable_send(segments, lost_on_first_attempt):
    # UDP style: send once, report only whatever actually arrived, no retry at all.
    return [segment for segment in segments if segment not in lost_on_first_attempt]


def reliable_send(segments, lost_on_first_attempt):
    # TCP style: keep retransmitting any segment that was not yet acknowledged.
    # In this simulation, anything lost on attempt 1 always succeeds on attempt 2.
    total_transmissions = len(segments)
    delivered = []
    needs_retransmit = []

    for segment in segments:
        if segment in lost_on_first_attempt:
            needs_retransmit.append(segment)
        else:
            delivered.append(segment)

    total_transmissions += len(needs_retransmit)
    delivered.extend(needs_retransmit)
    delivered.sort()

    return delivered, total_transmissions


def main():
    segments = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    lost_on_first_attempt = {2, 4}

    unreliable_result = unreliable_send(segments, lost_on_first_attempt)
    print("UDP style, single attempt, delivered:", unreliable_result)

    delivered, total_transmissions = reliable_send(segments, lost_on_first_attempt)
    print("TCP style, delivered:", delivered)
    print("TCP style, total transmissions used:", total_transmissions)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: Worked Example

A single application, a video conferencing platform, actually uses both protocols at once for genuinely different pieces of its own traffic. The live audio and video streams themselves travel over UDP, since a dropped frame should simply be skipped rather than retransmitted late. But the same platform's chat messages, sent alongside the call, travel over TCP, because a chat message that silently vanished would be a real, visible bug, not an acceptable trade off.

Signaling, the initial handshake that sets up who is calling whom and negotiates which media formats both sides support, also runs over TCP, since that exchange only happens once per call and correctness matters far more than the few milliseconds of setup delay. This split, UDP for the continuous, loss tolerant media stream and TCP for the infrequent, correctness critical control messages, is exactly how real video conferencing systems are built.

Even within the media stream itself, the platform layers its own lightweight reliability on top of UDP where it genuinely matters, periodically re-sending key frames so a viewer who just joined does not have to wait for the next scheduled one, without ever falling back to full TCP style retransmission for every single lost packet.

blocks.content: Practice

Take three real applications, a bank's mobile app, a live sports streaming service, and a multiplayer racing game, and for each one, decide whether its core data traffic should run over TCP or UDP, and explain specifically what would go visibly wrong if that choice were reversed.

Then extend the same exercise to a fourth, harder case: a voice assistant device that must both stream continuous audio to a cloud service and reliably deliver the occasional firmware update. Decide which protocol fits each of those two very different traffic types within the very same device, and justify the split the same way the video conferencing example did.
Key Takeaway

TCP and UDP solve the same problem, moving data between two applications, with deliberately opposite priorities. TCP's handshake, acknowledgments, retransmission, flow control, and congestion control turn unreliable IP into a clean, ordered stream at the cost of setup time and potential delay, exactly what banking, SSH, and file transfers need. UDP skips all of that entirely, accepting loss in exchange for speed and freshness, exactly what DNS, live video, and gaming need, leaving any reliability the application actually wants to be built on top, deliberately, rather than assumed. QUIC shows the two ideas can combine, UDP's speed with TCP style reliability built independently per stream, avoiding head of line blocking altogether.
